content: 1. This document provides a list of frequently asked questions (FAQs) encountered during the editing of pages related to the Infectious Disease Project. Each question is followed by a recommended course of action. 2. FAQ 1: What should I do if there are no references on a page? Do not edit, remove, or add references that already have an existing link. If a reference contains a broken link, delete both the reference and the sentence that was cited using that reference. 3. FAQ 2: What should I do if there is no page for the organism? Verify the spelling of the organism's name. If you are redirected, check whether the organism is already categorized under the Causes microchapter. If neither of these options resolves the issue, email one of the deputy editors-in-chief to review your request. 4. FAQ 3: What should I do if there is no page for the disease? If the organism page contains only basic information about the pathogen without clinical content, do not create a microchapter for the disease. If the disease content spans five A4-length pages or more, create a microchapter for the disease. If the disease content is less than five A4-length pages, do not create a microchapter for the disease. 5. FAQ 4: How should I name a disease page? Use a clear and specific naming convention, such as Staphylococcus aureus infection. 6. FAQ 5: What should I do if there is no Synonyms and Keywords section? Use the Synonyms and Keywords template and list the synonyms after it. Ensure that each synonym or keyword added redirects to the page name. 7. FAQ 6: What should I do if Wikipedia content is newer than the content on WikiDoc? Do not add content from Wikipedia to WikiDoc. WikiDoc pages containing Wikipedia content will eventually be replaced with peer-reviewed, medical-level content for quality assurance. 8. FAQ 7: What should I do if multiple organisms cause the same disease? Use the new template available at the top of the Home Page for that disease. At the bottom of the Home Page, add a Related Chapters subheading after the Case Studies subheading and list the same organisms mentioned earlier. Do not redirect the Causes page. Instead, add the Related Chapters tag at the bottom of the Causes page as well. If the Causes page contains a list of causes, ensure that the organisms you added are also included in the list. 9. FAQ 8: What should I do if a page is not microchaptered? Do not microchapter the page yourself. Inform one of the deputy editors-in-chief about the issue. If the organism page contains only basic information about the pathogen without clinical content, do not microchapter the page. If the disease content spans five A4-length pages or more, create a microchapter for the disease. If the disease content is less than five A4-length pages, do not create a microchapter for the disease. 10. FAQ 9: What should I do if a page is empty? Refer to the Patient Information microchapter of the disease for the information you need. If there is no Patient Information page, consult the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) website for the required information. Ensure that you cite the CDC page appropriately after using its information. If the information is not available on either the Patient Information microchapter or the CDC page, communicate your concern with a deputy editor-in-chief, who can assist in obtaining the information from reliable peer-reviewed medical journals. When citing medical journals, ensure proper citation to avoid plagiarism. Refer to the Editor's Help Menu to understand the content that should be included in each microchapter. Learn how to cite references properly by clicking the provided link. Learn how to avoid plagiarism while citing by clicking the provided link.
